The Ni-Co based superalloy has a high degree of alloying, with Al + Ti contents around 7.5 wt%.

The as-cast microstructure of the directionally solidified Ni-Co based superalloy exhibits a typical columnar-grained structure with an average primary and secondary dendrite arm spacing of 363 ± 6 μm and 74 ± 2 μm, respectively.
The main precipitates in the as-cast microstructure are the rosette-shaped (γ + γ') eutectic and the lath-shaped η-Ni3Ti phase.
The EPMA results show that Ti is severely segregated in the eutectic (γ + γ') and η phases, while Al tends to be uniformly distributed between the eutectic and the γ matrix.
The segregation coefficients (k) indicate that W and Ti have the greatest tendency to segregate, with k values of 1.65 and 0.49, respectively.
After homogenization at 1180°C for 2 hours, the dendritic segregation is almost eliminated, and only a few small particulate phases remain in the interdendritic region.

The optimal single-stage homogenization process for this Ni-Co based superalloy is determined to be 1180°C for 2 hours, as it provides sufficient diffusion to eliminate dendritic segregation without excessive grain growth.
The diffusion coefficients of W and Ti at 1180°C were estimated to be 11.02 × 10^-15 m^2/s and 11.97 × 10^-15 m^2/s, respectively, using a kinetic diffusion model.

The strongly segregated element Ti, which is continuously rejected into the remaining liquid during γ matrix solidification, contributes to the formation of the eutectic (γ + γ') and the transformation of the η phase.

Compared to the traditional melting process, the Ni-Co based superalloy produced by directional solidification has a simpler microstructure, without the presence of irregular MC-type carbides and Zr-rich phases.

The directionally solidified Ni-Co based superalloy has a lower deformation activation energy and deformation resistance compared to equiaxed grain alloys, due to the optimal deformation direction in the directionally solidified columnar grains.
The homogenization process eliminates the eutectic phase, reduces element segregation, and produces a more uniform microstructure, which improves the hot formability of the as-cast superalloy.
Excessive homogenization can lead to grain coarsening, which decreases the thermoplasticity and yield of the final workpiece.

The diffusion coefficients of the strongly segregated elements, such as W and Ti, provide a theoretical basis for optimizing the homogenization process and understanding the kinetics of element redistribution.
The directional solidification process can avoid the formation of bulk η phase and carbon nitride strips, resulting in excellent hot-working plasticity for the Ni-Co based superalloy.
